title: Mixed conditionals
theme: Mixed conditionals + counterfactuals + inversion in conditionals + alternatives to "if"
goal: Student handles complex hypothetical structures fluently — mixing time references, inverting for formal effect, and using alternatives to "if".
module_chunks: If I had + past participle, I would be + base now (past → present)
If I were + adj/noun, I would have + past participle (present → past)
Were I to do that... (inverted hypothetical future)
Should you need... (inverted first conditional, formal)
Provided that / As long as / Unless

units.title: Past condition, present result
units.grammar_focus: Mixed conditional past → present (If I had + pp, I would + base now)
units.real_life_context: You connect a past action to its present consequence — how your present would differ if your past had differed.

grammar.sentence: If I had studied medicine, I _____ in a hospital now.
grammar.explanation: Mixed conditional with past condition affecting present result. The marker "now" anchors the result in the present, so use "would + base" — not "would have been" (pure third) or "will be" (first).

grammar.sentence: She wouldn't be exhausted right now if she _____ overtime last night.
grammar.explanation: Past cause needs past perfect in the if-clause: "hadn't / had not worked overtime last night". The present effect ("wouldn't / would not be exhausted") signals the mixed form.

grammar.sentence: If we had bought that house in 2010, we _____ enough equity to retire by now.
grammar.explanation: Past cause ("had bought") + present result ("would have enough equity now"). Note: "have" here is the stative present verb, not "have + past participle".

grammar.sentence: If I had studied medicine, I would have been a doctor now.
grammar.hint: For a present state, use "would be" — not "would have been"
grammar.answer: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.
grammar.explanation: "Would have been" places the result fully in the past (pure third conditional). The marker "now" requires a present consequence, so use "would be" — the mixed form. Common C1 trap.

grammar.passage: Linguists often note that bilingual children process language differently. Had Maria's parents spoken Portuguese to her at home, she would likely be fluent today. Instead, she has spent the last two years catching up on a language her own family treats as second nature.
grammar.question: Why isn't Maria fluent in Portuguese today, according to the passage?
grammar.answer: her parents didn't speak Portuguese to her at home
accepts: they didn't speak it at home
grammar.explanation: The inverted third conditional "Had Maria's parents spoken..." reveals the unmet past condition. The mixed form ("would likely be fluent today") makes the present consequence explicit.

listening_speaking.text: If I had studied medicine, I'd be a doctor now.
She wouldn't be tired if she hadn't worked overtime.
If we'd bought back then, we'd own outright today.
I wouldn't be here if I hadn't met him in college.
If you hadn't introduced us, we'd still be strangers.

units.title: Present state, past result
units.grammar_focus: Mixed conditional present → past (If I were + adj, I would have + pp)
units.real_life_context: You explain a past outcome by appealing to a permanent or ongoing trait — "if I weren't so X, I wouldn't have done Y".

grammar.sentence: If she weren't so stubborn, she _____ to a compromise weeks ago.
grammar.explanation: Mixed reversed form: present trait ("weren't / were not so stubborn") with a past result ("weeks ago"). Past result requires "would have + past participle".

grammar.sentence: If I _____ a morning person, I would have accepted that early meeting yesterday.
grammar.explanation: "Were" (subjunctive across all persons) marks a present/ongoing trait in the if-clause. The trait explains why the past action didn't happen.

grammar.sentence: If he weren't less sensitive, he _____ that comment so personally last week.
grammar.explanation: Ongoing personality (present) explains last week's reaction (past). Mixed: present condition → past result with "would have + past participle".

grammar.sentence: If I weren't allergic to nuts, I would eat that cake at the party.
grammar.hint: The cake was at a past party — the result should also be past
grammar.answer: If I weren't allergic to nuts, I would have eaten that cake at the party.
grammar.explanation: The allergy is permanent (present condition, "weren't / were not"), but the cake event was a specific past moment ("at the party"). Past result requires "would have eaten", not "would eat".

grammar.passage: Engineers tend to overplan. If our lead developer weren't so detail-obsessed, we would have shipped the prototype three months ago. As it stands, we're still polishing edges that no user will ever see.
grammar.question: Why hasn't the prototype shipped yet?
grammar.answer: the lead developer is too detail-obsessed
grammar.explanation: The permanent trait ("weren't / were not so detail-obsessed") explains the past failure ("would have shipped three months ago"). Mixed conditional in action.

listening_speaking.text: If she weren't so stubborn, she'd have agreed by now.
If I weren't allergic, I would have tried it.
He'd have called you back if he were less anxious.
If we weren't on a tight budget, we'd have flown business.
If she weren't so generous, she'd have kept the prize money.

units.title: Had I known (inverted)
units.grammar_focus: Inverted third conditional (Had I known... / Had she said...)
units.real_life_context: You speak or write with formal-literary register, dropping "if" and inverting the auxiliary.

grammar.sentence: _____ earlier, I would have caught the train.
grammar.explanation: Inverted third conditional drops "if" and brings the auxiliary "had" before the subject: "Had I left" = "If I had left". Formal, literary, common in spoken English when adding gravity.

grammar.sentence: _____ the offer, she'd be running the team now.
grammar.explanation: "Had + subject + past participle" — inverted form. Note the mixed conditional consequence ("she'd / she would be running the team now") — inversion works across third and mixed conditionals.

grammar.sentence: _____ what I know now, I would have left that company years ago.
grammar.explanation: "Had I known" — inverted form of "If I had known". Inversion drops "if" and brings the auxiliary "had" before the subject.

grammar.sentence: If had I known, I would have told you.
grammar.answer: Had I known, I would have told you.
accepts: If I had known, I would have told you.
grammar.explanation: You can either use "if + had + subject" OR invert ("had + subject" without "if"). Mixing both — "if had I" — is ungrammatical. Inversion replaces "if".

grammar.passage: The architect's notebook reveals a single regret. 'Had I trusted my first instinct,' she wrote, 'the building would stand differently today.' Critics now agree that the compromise version softened what could have been her boldest work.
grammar.question: What does the architect regret?
grammar.explanation: "Had I trusted" — inverted regret. The mixed conditional consequence ("would stand differently today") connects past hesitation to present reality.

listening_speaking.text: Had I known, I would have called you sooner.
Had she accepted, she'd be a partner today.
Had we left ten minutes earlier, we'd have made it.
Had he asked, I would have helped without hesitation.
Had they listened, the project wouldn't have failed.

units.title: Were I to, Should you
units.grammar_focus: Inverted hypotheticals — "Were I to + base" (formal future hypothetical) and "Should you + base" (formal first conditional)
units.real_life_context: You write formal proposals, emails, contracts — registering the hypothetical with elevated diction.

grammar.sentence: _____ to accept the offer, I would relocate next month.
grammar.explanation: "Were I to + base" is the inverted second conditional, formal/literary. It signals a hypothetical future action you're entertaining. Equivalent to "If I were to accept..." but more elegant.

grammar.sentence: _____ any further questions, please contact our office.
grammar.explanation: "Should you + base" — inverted first conditional, very formal. Used in business correspondence to signal possibility ("if you happen to have"). Common in customer service writing.

grammar.sentence: _____ to ask me, I'd say the proposal needs more work.
grammar.explanation: "Were you to ask me" = "If you were to ask me". Hedged offer of opinion, formal register.

grammar.sentence: Should I had known, I would have come earlier.
grammar.hint: "Should" pairs with present-form base, not past perfect
grammar.answer: Had I known, I would have come earlier.
grammar.explanation: "Should + subject + base" is for first conditional (present/future hypotheticals). For past hypotheticals, switch to "Had + subject + past participle". Don't mix the two patterns.

grammar.passage: The contract reads, in its closing clause: 'Were either party to withdraw before completion, the deposit shall be forfeit. Should circumstances require an extension, the parties may renegotiate in good faith.' The language is deliberately old-fashioned — clarity dressed as ceremony.
grammar.question: What happens if a party withdraws early?
grammar.explanation: "Were either party to withdraw" — inverted second conditional. "Shall be forfeit" — formal passive future. The whole clause demonstrates legal-register inversion.

listening_speaking.text: Were I to accept, I'd start in June.
Should you need help, just ask.
Were you to ask me, I'd say no.
Should anything change, we'll let you know.
Were she to apply, she'd have a strong case.

units.title: Suppose, But for, Unless
units.grammar_focus: Alternatives to "if" — suppose/supposing, but for + noun, without, unless, provided that
units.real_life_context: You diversify hypothetical scaffolding away from "if" — for nuance, register, or emphasis.

grammar.sentence: _____ you found a wallet on the street — what would you do?
grammar.explanation: "Suppose" (or "Supposing") opens a hypothetical scenario conversationally, replacing "if" with a softer, more inviting framing. Common in story prompts and thought experiments.

grammar.sentence: _____ his support, we wouldn't have launched on time.
grammar.explanation: "But for + noun" = "if it hadn't / had not been for + noun". Formal, slightly literary. "But for his support" = without his support, in the past hypothetical sense. Pairs with third conditional result.

grammar.sentence: We'll go ahead _____ the weather doesn't turn.
grammar.explanation: "Provided that" = "if (and only if)". Formal "if" with the added flavor of a condition that must hold. "Unless" would invert the logic ("unless it turns"); "provided that" preserves it.

grammar.sentence: Unless you don't tell me the truth, I can't help you.
grammar.answer: Unless you tell me the truth, I can't help you.
grammar.explanation: "Unless" = "if... not". Double-negative ("unless you don't / do not") flips meaning back to positive — saying you must lie. Drop the redundant "don't / do not".

grammar.passage: Suppose for a moment that the city had invested in flood barriers a decade ago. But for that investment, last year's storm would have done ten times more damage. The cost-benefit is rarely visible until disaster arrives — or doesn't.
grammar.question: What hypothetically prevented worse damage from last year's storm?
grammar.answer: the investment in flood barriers a decade ago
grammar.explanation: "Suppose" opens the hypothetical; "But for that investment" gestures at the counterfactual ("if it weren't / were not for that investment, the damage would have been ten times worse"). C1 phrasing layering two alternatives to "if".

listening_speaking.text: Suppose you found a wallet — what would you do?
But for his support, I wouldn't be here.
Unless we leave now, we'll miss it.
Provided that the budget holds, we'll launch in May.
Without coffee, I'd have collapsed by noon.

cross_unit_consolidation: Form mixed conditionals in both directions (past→present and present→past)
Invert second conditionals formally ("Were I to..." / "Should you...")
Replace "if" with suppose, but for, unless, provided that, as long as, without
Distinguish "would be" (present result) from "would have been" (past result)
Use subjunctive "were" across all persons without lapsing to "was"
